Q: how to type certain commands in vim, like CTRL-] ^Wc etc.. on a German Keyboard A:

On Linux there is a "de-us" layout. It's qwerty but you can still write umlauts by combining with AltGr.

Q: Measuring computation time A:

Measuring performance can be tricky on modern processors because for example many of them have a variable clock speed.

This means that they're normally going slow because no CPU is needed and they can use less energy and generate less heat that way.

When you require an heavy computation the OS detects that now there is work for the CPU and can increase the clock speed (and heat and current) to get the results faster.

To avoid this specific problem you should measure clock cycles used by your computation instead of cpu time (or worse wall clock time). A good profiler should give you this option (I'm using oprofile).

Q: read-syntax: `#...=` forms not enabled A:

One approach to enabling support for self-referential graphs in Racket code is to use a reader extension to call read-syntax on one with support for them enabled via the read-syntax-accept-graph parameter.

Create a file named graph-reader.rkt for the extension module:

#lang racket/base

(require racket/syntax-srcloc)
(provide read (rename-out [read-syntax/graph read-syntax]))

(define (read-syntax/graph src in)
  (parameterize ([read-syntax-accept-graph #t])
    (let* ([stx (read-syntax src in)]
           [datum (syntax->datum stx)])
      ;; unlike when using read, the graph has to be explicitly instantiated.
      (datum->syntax stx (make-reader-graph datum) (syntax-srcloc stx)))))

Then you can use the extension in other source files immediately before the graph expression:

(displayln "Testing self-referential reading... ")

(let ((a #reader "graph-reader.rkt" #0='(0 . #0#)))
  (println (car a)))

(println #reader "graph-reader.rkt" '(#1=100 #1# #1# #2=150 #2#))

will print out

Testing self-referential reading... 
0
'(100 100 100 150 150)

The documentation suggests this is a bad idea

In read-syntax mode, graph structure is parsed the same way as in read mode. However, since syntax objects made from plain S-expressions may not contain cycles, each #‹digit10›{1,8}= definition and #‹digit10›{1,8}# reference is replaced with a placeholder in the result that contains the referenced value. Since such syntax objects are not directly useful (they cannot be marshaled to compiled code and are therefore rejected by the default compilation handler), parsing of graph structure in read-syntax mode is controlled by the separate read-syntax-accept-graph parameter, which is initially set to #f.

but my (admittedly limited) testing showed that at least simple code using it can be compiled (Via raco make) to binary and executed. It's possible that more complicated data structures will cause issues; such graphs are probably better off being built manually using placeholder functions, even if it is more awkward and less clear to write than the shorthand notation.

Q: "Call to a member function generate()" error emitted when trying to load CodeIgniter's table library from a view file A:

That is one wrong approach to MVC architecture. You don't need to load the library in the view, because all views are loaded from one controller, so every external helper or library should be loaded from the controller and then used or sent to the views.
